cases.name: 12 Maple Avenue — Remix Properties Restaurant Parking Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant proposed rehabilitating an 1820s house at 12 Maple Avenue into a farm-to-table restaurant (144 seats, both indoor and outdoor) requiring a 33-space parking variance (15 on-site vs. 48 required), to be offset via a lease/valet agreement with the adjacent 20 Maple Avenue lot bringing effective capacity to roughly 33-55 spaces depending on stacking and valet. The applicant presented extensive parking-utilization, foot-traffic, and staff-carpooling data, plus over 500 petition signatures of local support. A nearby shopping-center (Armonk Square) managing partner objected, raising concerns about spillover parking, added liability, plowing/maintenance costs, and enforcement burden on his own lot, though he said he supported the restaurant concept generally. Because the Planning Board's own traffic consultant (H&H, reviewing the applicant's Kimberly-Horn study) had only just responded and the Board had not had time to review it, the hearing was adjourned rather than decided, with the case to return once the Planning Board weighs in (expected around its September 28 meeting).
The applicant requested and received a further adjournment of its parking-variance hearing to the November meeting; no new substantive discussion occurred at this session.
The applicant requested a further adjournment to the December meeting; no new substantive discussion occurred.

After three prior adjournments, the applicant returned with a signed parking agreement with Armonk Square (resolving that neighbor's earlier objection) and a lease at 20 Maple Avenue providing 22-32 spaces, plus a letter of intent for overflow employee parking at the American Legion site. With valet, the applicant projected 56 total available spaces against a 48-space requirement (33-space variance from the 15 on-site spaces). A young Armonk resident spoke in support, arguing modern dining patterns (rideshare and carpooling) reduce real parking demand below the code formula. The Board approved the 33-space variance unanimously, conditioning it on town-attorney review and approval of all referenced parking agreements and on compliance with whatever traffic/parking determinations the Planning Board makes during site plan review.

cases.name: 873 North Broadway — Restaurant/Brewery Parking Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a parking variance of 26 spaces (46 required by code based on floor area, 20 provided on-site) for a new restaurant with accessory brewing/tap room capped at 45 seated diners, backed by a Planning Board referral and a parking consultant's analysis estimating a real peak demand of only ~33 vehicles (to be met via valet stacking and a leased overflow lot). Neighboring property owners raised concerns about evening headlight/traffic intrusion through an access easement and cited an existing rear-lot easement dispute; a board member (Les Berkelhamer) pressed for independent Route 22 traffic-volume data rather than relying on the Planning Board's ongoing traffic review, triggering a lengthy disagreement with the Town Attorney over the ZBA's obligation to develop its own evidentiary record. Board member John Stipo stated outright opposition. The application was tabled to the February 3 meeting so the applicant could supply NYSDOT traffic-count data on North Broadway.

Continuing from January, the applicant submitted NYSDOT hourly traffic-volume data for North Broadway showing volumes peak at over 2,000 vehicles/hour from 5-6pm but drop to about half that by the restaurant's 7-8pm dinner peak, and that the restaurant itself would add only about seven trips per hour — addressing the traffic concern raised at the prior meeting. The board negotiated a detailed condition set (45-seat maximum at all times regardless of indoor/outdoor seating, no standing bar service, valet and off-site tandem parking limited to the rear lot, leased off-site employee parking at 11 Washington Place on nights/weekends, a dinner reservations policy, incorporation of the applicant's traffic and parking management plan, and conditioning the variance on Planning Board site plan approval). A board member's push for a mandatory 6pm reservation start time and a request to keep the existing no-left-turn restriction on the driveway exit were both declined as unnecessary given the de minimis traffic impact. The board granted the 26-space parking variance, finding the five statutory variance factors satisfied notwithstanding the size of the variance, with John Stipo dissenting.

cases.name: Grove Road/Palmer Avenue Corner Lot — One-Space Parking Area & Coverage Variance
cases.address: 30 Palmer Avenue (corner lot fronting Grove Road), White Plains, NY
cases.applicant: Property owner referred to in testimony as "Tony"/"Mr. Colton" and his wife (ASR renders the name inconsistently)

timeline.summary: Renewed application (scaled down from an original 3-space, then 2-space, concept previously denied by this board in 2017 and challenged in NY State Supreme Court) for a single off-street parking space requiring a stopping-sight-distance variance (approximately 134 ft available vs. 200 ft required looking south, and roughly 105-218 ft depending on measurement method looking north) plus a modest (~138 sq ft) gross land coverage variance for an elevated, walled parking area with guide rail and screening. The applicant argued that a subsequently-adopted town no-parking zone on Grove Road (installed for fire/emergency-access safety reasons after a police department study) strengthened the application by removing the on-street-parking-loss objection from the prior denial, and presented an updated site-distance letter from the town's traffic consultant. Multiple neighbors objected at length, arguing the retaining wall and vegetation would block the very sight lines the applicant relied on, that the structure was oversized for one car, that neighborhood character and property values would suffer, and that the applicant already had a usable one-car garage. After extensive, often heated back-and-forth on code interpretation and history, the board closed the public hearing but reserved its decision for the following meeting, with both sides permitted to submit final photographic evidence.

Deliberating on the evidence closed at the prior meeting, the board treated the stopping-sight-distance variance and the gross land coverage variance as two separate votes, noting both had to pass for the project to proceed. On sight distance, the board found the applicant's and the town's traffic consultants had adequately addressed safety, that a similar variance had recently been granted elsewhere, and that reducing the request from three spaces to one was a meaningful accommodation; it granted that variance unanimously (5-0). On land coverage, two members (Les Berkelhamer and John Stipo) argued the elevated parking structure was built oversized for a single car and that its coverage overage was unwarranted; the remaining three members found the impervious-surface increase de minimis and outweighed by the benefit to the applicant, and the variance passed 3-2.

cases.name: Summit Club Partners LLC — 570 Bedford Road — Temporary Construction Signage Variance

timeline.summary: As part of a 73-unit residential site plan under Planning Board review, the applicant sought a fence-height variance to install 10-foot fencing around new tennis/pickleball courts (6 feet is the code maximum), citing the need to contain flying balls; the applicant noted the property's prior tennis courts had also had a 10-foot fence. The board found the fencing well set back from Bedford Road and screened by proposed landscaping, with no undesirable change to neighborhood character, and granted the variance unanimously.

Developer of a 72-unit condominium/golf-club community sought variances to erect an oversized (24 sq ft vs. 6 sq ft permitted) temporary entry sign at the property line (0 ft vs. 10 ft setback) during a multi-year construction and marketing period, after the Building Inspector rejected the applicant's argument that the mixed residential/golf-club project should be classified under commercial signage rules (which would have allowed a larger sign without a variance). The Town Planner agreed the site functioned more like a commercial/golf-course property than a typical residential lot, making the standard small residential sign inadequate for marketing purposes; screening and setback from Route 22 would minimize any impact, including on oncoming headlights. The Board upheld the Building Inspector's technical determination but found the variance appropriate given the site's effectively mixed-use character, granting it unanimously.

cases.name: 428–436 Main Street (corner of Maple Ave) — Parking Variance
cases.applicant: 428-436 Main Street property owner, represented by attorney Daniel Hollis

timeline.summary: The applicant initially sought an interpretation that a 1996 area variance already excused the property (a century-old, multi-store/apartment commercial building at a prominent Main Street corner) from site plan, permit, and parking requirements for a re-rented retail unit, after a building inspector notice of violation. At the Town Attorney's suggestion, the applicant instead pursued a fresh area variance covering the entire building's parking shortfall (20 spaces required, zero legally striped/compliant spaces existing, though 11 undifferentiated spaces exist informally) and withdrew the interpretation request without prejudice, with the intent of finally resolving recurring parking variance battles each time a tenant turns over and clearing the way for Planning Board site plan approval covering all the building's stores and the apartment. The board found the variance mathematically substantial (effectively 100%) but mitigated by a century of the building operating without incident despite the parking deficiency, no feasible alternative short of demolition, and no environmental impact, and granted it unanimously.

The applicant sought to expand a prior 20-space parking variance to 24 spaces to cover a vacant retail unit under its most parking-intensive potential use (a beauty parlor), consolidating the building's parking needs so future tenants would not need to return to the ZBA/planning board each time. Ed Lashins argued at length that several existing, code-noncompliant spaces behind the building (already informally used for parking) should be recognized and reduce the size of the variance needed, and a nearby property owner (representing 12 Maple Avenue) urged the board to make participation in a future downtown parking district a condition. After extended debate, the applicant agreed to scale back to a 22-space variance (matching what the planning board had already indicated it would accept), and the board voted to approve 22 spaces, adopting the findings from the prior year's 20-space resolution.

cases.name: Basis Industrial Acquisitions LLC — FAR & Parking Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 0.13 FAR variance (0.43 proposed vs. 0.3 permitted) and a 57-space off-street parking variance (220 provided vs. 277 required) for a self-storage warehouse building. Counsel requested an adjournment before any discussion; the Board adjourned the hearing without deliberation.

After months of negotiation with neighbors, the applicant returned having eliminated the previously-requested 57-space parking variance entirely (now zoning-compliant on parking) and reduced the FAR variance from 0.13 to 0.08 (0.38 proposed vs. 0.3 permitted). One neighbor's representative expressed continued reservations but ultimately voiced support for the reduced request; another neighbor (Arrow Hardware) supported it through a representative. The Board found the variance now de minimis given the concessions, the cleanup of the physical site, and lack of any shown environmental impact, and granted it unanimously by a 3-0 vote of the members present.

cases.name: Robert Levine — Piping Brook Lane, Bedford — Certificate of Occupancy Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant's counsel requested an adjournment of the public hearing to the May 25 meeting; no substantive discussion occurred.

Applicant, who built the house in 1987 and two sheds in 2010, sought gross-land-coverage (6,363 sq ft) and side-yard-setback (6.3 ft) variances to obtain a long-outstanding certificate of occupancy; the sheds sit within the setback and encroach have existed without incident for over a decade. A neighbor's letter raised a separate, unrelated complaint about landscaping encroachment onto a conservation-easement area, which the applicant agreed to resolve before the Conservation Board as a condition of the variance. The Board granted the variance unanimously, conditioned on compliance with whatever the Conservation Board later requires.

cases.name: 42 Sarles Street — North Castle 42 LLC Generator Setback Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant, who purchased the property in October 2021, sought a variance from the code requirement that an owner hold title for two years before establishing an accessory apartment in an existing c.1900 accessory structure, being about five months short. Applicant's counsel argued the two-year rule itself had little rational basis; the Board agreed the shortfall was de minimis, self-created only in a technical sense, and had no impact on neighborhood character, and granted the variance unanimously.

In an R2A district, applicant sought a front-yard setback variance of 53'10" (150 ft required for generators, roughly triple the standard 50-ft front setback, 96'2" provided) under Town Code 355-15(Q)(2) to install a generator near existing pool-house mechanical equipment, represented by attorney Corey Salum. The board questioned the propane fuel source and clustering rationale; counsel explained the generator was sited near the existing heat pump/pool equipment to minimize utility runs, with substantial screening and the nearest house about 320 feet away. No neighbor objections were received. Approved 3-0.

cases.name: 15 Wampus Lake Drive — Lally Pool/Patio Land Coverage Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a gross land coverage variance of 9,921 sq ft (18,628 sq ft permitted, 28,549 sq ft proposed) under Town Code 355-26(A) to add a pool and patio to a property whose land coverage was already roughly 7,000 sq ft over the limit due to a large, 50-year-old preexisting driveway (documented via historical GIS imagery), not created by the current owner. The board, applying the legal standard that a variance must be the minimum necessary, pushed the applicant's engineer to identify feasible reductions — ultimately agreeing to remove a roughly 1,200 sq ft gravel area and explore shrinking sections of the driveway — and directed the applicant to return the following month with a redesigned, smaller variance request rather than approving that night.

Carried over from February, applicant sought a gross land coverage variance under Town Code 355-26 for a new gunite pool at an existing single-family home in an R2A district. In response to board feedback at the prior meeting, the applicant's representative revised the plan to remove 3,118 sq ft of an oversized, decades-old nonconforming driveway (giving up drive access to a rear garage, now to be used only as storage), reducing the requested variance from 9,921 sq ft to 6,803 sq ft, and actually decreasing overall existing land coverage. No neighbor objections or new notice were required since the request shrank. Approved unanimously.

cases.name: 63 Overlook Road — Mullane/Baldisaro Deck Rebuild Variance
cases.address: 63 Overlook Road, North White Plains, NY

timeline.summary: Applicants sought a rear-yard setback variance and gross land coverage variance to replace a deteriorated deck with a deeper one. During the hearing, the board discovered the published notice (based on subtracting from the existing nonconforming setback rather than the code-required standard) understated the needed variance as 8.3 feet when the correct figure is 16.3 feet (30 ft required, 13.7 ft proposed). The board directed the applicant to re-notice with the corrected figures and adjourned the matter to April.

In an R-10 district, applicants sought a rear-yard setback variance of 16.3 feet (30 ft required, 13.7 ft provided) and a gross land coverage variance of roughly 703 sq ft (56,50 sq ft area basis) under Town Code 355-21 and 355-26(C) to rebuild an existing deteriorated deck about 7.4 feet deeper, represented by architect Arbin Salah. The deck footprint remains pre-existing nonconforming and the upper balcony is not being enlarged. The board found the roughly 12% coverage variance not substantial and no negative neighborhood character impact. Approved unanimously 3-0.

cases.name: 16 Davis Drive — Gross Land Coverage & Building Height Variance (Goudus)
cases.lastStatus: partially granted — coverage variance approved; height variance held in abeyance

trajectory.status: partially granted — coverage variance approved; height variance held in abeyance

timeline.summary: The applicants sought a gross land-coverage variance (6,940 square feet over the allowable 26,251) for a three-car garage addition, driveway resurfacing/widening, and other improvements. A directly-adjacent neighbor raised serious concerns: fill had been brought onto the site without a permit near Westmoreland Sanctuary (a shared preserve with Bedford), triggering a town-wide stop-work order, and the regraded driveway would raise headlight glare toward his home. The board declined to vote without the Conservation Board's review (not scheduled until September) and a final sign-off letter from the Town's outside engineer (Kellard Sessions), and adjourned the matter, with a suggestion that the case might need to be re-noticed if materials were not ready by October.

timeline.status: partially granted — coverage variance approved; height variance held in abeyance
timeline.summary: Returning after the August adjournment, the applicant's engineer presented drainage redesigns developed with the Town's outside engineer (Kellard Sessions) and the Conservation Board, including a relocated and enlarged drainage pond and new inlet piping to redirect runoff away from the adjoining neighbor's yard toward Westmoreland Sanctuary; the neighbor indicated satisfaction with the drainage solution and asked for additional deer-resistant screening, which the applicant agreed to coordinate informally. The board approved the 6,940-square-foot gross land coverage variance. However, it balked at a separate 6.69-foot building height variance needed only because of a roughly nine-foot glass "skylight" roof projection, with members arguing the architectural feature could be built lower without losing its function and that visibility from Route 22 made it a troubling precedent for the town's 30-foot height limit. Rather than deny it, the board approved the coverage variance and left the height variance open, inviting the applicant to return with a redesign (and their architect) after further discussion.

cases.name: Meda Property — Accessory Apartment Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant's counsel (Kory Salomone, Zarin & Steinmetz) asked the board to remove a condition from a prior coverage-variance resolution barring residential use above a detached garage/accessory structure built in 1997, and to grant a new variance allowing an accessory apartment there (structures built after 1984 otherwise being ineligible) so Meda's mother-in-law could live on site. The board pressed on why square footage figures for added habitable space differed between last year's and this year's applications (roughly 1,193 vs. 2,479 sq ft) and expressed concern that the property's septic capacity for the resulting six-to-seven-bedroom total hadn't been documented, given Meda had previously told the board the space would only be used as an office. The board voted 4-0 to correct a drafting error in the prior resolution (substituting "planning board" for "town board" as the approving body for any future accessory apartment) but adjourned the substantive accessory-apartment request to the January meeting, asking the applicant to reconcile the square-footage numbers and submit Health Department documentation of septic approval for the added bedrooms.

Continuing from the December meeting, the applicant's team presented documentation of an approved eight-bedroom septic system and an explanation that the earlier square-footage discrepancy reflected different metrics (land coverage vs. floor area) rather than a real change in plans. Ed Lashins said his prior questions had not fully been answered but agreed to move forward; the board reopened and closed the public hearing and made detailed findings on the five area-variance factors before voting 5-0 to approve, conditioned on any third-party (non-family) lease being for a term of at least one year to guard against transient/short-term rental use.

cases.name: 76 Virginia Road — National Lawn Sprinkler FAR Variance
cases.applicant: John Luciano (National Lawn Sprinkler Co.), represented by Tony Veneziano

timeline.summary: The applicant sought a floor-area-ratio variance (reduced during the hearing from 0.15 to 0.12 over, i.e. FAR of 0.72 vs. 0.6 permitted) to build a truck-storage/office building for a landscaping business, requiring significant rock excavation and hillside blasting or mechanical chipping on a site near Miller Hill. Neighbors from the Miller Hill area raised safety and property-damage concerns about the excavation method, and board member Robert Greer pushed for a completed geotechnical report (from a town-retained New Jersey firm) and neighbor insurance protections before any vote. With Ed Lashins recused (business relationship with the applicant) and Scott Stopnik absent, only three members remained and the board lacked the quorum needed to act; the hearing was adjourned to the May 1 meeting pending the planning board's site plan process and the geotechnical report.

Continuing from April, the applicant reported that the planning board had retained an outside geotechnical firm (Carlin Simpson) to critique the site engineer's work, that the applicant's team would prefer mechanical chipping over blasting (in line with neighbor preference), and that both mandatory and additional voluntary insurance would protect Miller Hill neighbors during excavation, all to be finalized as conditions of planning board site plan approval. With those process assurances and no neighbors present to object, the board closed the hearing and voted to approve the 0.6-to-0.72 FAR variance, with John Stipo abstaining because he had missed part of the prior discussion.

cases.name: Dempsey Property — Gross Land Coverage Variance (Pool/Pool House)

timeline.summary: Continuation of a previously-approved swing pool/pool house project; applicant requested a de minimis 421-square-foot gross land coverage variance (existing 14,481 sq ft, up to 14,902 sq ft required) to complete the approved landscaping/screening (a planted berm and privacy fence). No neighbor feedback was received. The board found no change to neighborhood character, no feasible alternative, and no environmental impact, and granted the variance unanimously.

cases.name: Costa Residence — Gross Land Coverage Variance for Pool/Patio

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 1,709.1 sq ft gross land coverage variance (maximum allowed 9,480.9 sq ft; 11,285 sq ft proposed) to install a 16x40 in-ground pool and patio on an R1A corner lot; the applicant argued permeable paving and pool water offset much of the added coverage. No neighbor objections were raised. The board found the request comparable to the prior case, not substantial relative to the amount required, self-created but not disqualifying, and with no adverse neighborhood impact, and granted it unanimously by roll call.

cases.name: Deck Extension — Side Yard Setback Variance
cases.address: Address unclear from ASR (rendered as "9 Quaker Meeting House"), R1A district

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 4-foot-6-inch side yard setback variance (25 feet required, 21.5 feet — or per a correction, 21.6 feet — proposed) to extend an existing deck toward a wetland-adjacent rear yard, with the extension screened from neighbors on both sides. No board questions or public objections were raised, consistent with the board's pattern of quickly approving de minimis, unopposed variances that night.

cases.name: 120 Lafayette Avenue — Off-Street Parking & Backing-Into-Right-of-Way Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 17-space off-street parking variance and a variance to permit vehicles to continue backing into the Lafayette Avenue right-of-way, formalizing a parking practice reportedly in place for about 30 years, to enable installation of rooftop solar panels. The Planning Board positively recommended the variance, and counsel cited a similar variance granted at 77 Lafayette Avenue in 2020 as precedent. The board found no change to neighborhood character on an already busy commercial street, no substantial impact, and granted the variance unanimously by roll call.

cases.name: 121 Lafayette Avenue — Off-Street Parking & Backing-Into-Right-of-Way Variance

timeline.summary: Companion application to the 120 Lafayette Avenue matter, seeking a 4-space off-street parking variance and the same right-of-way backing variance to formalize longstanding parking practice ahead of a solar panel installation; the board applied the identical five-factor analysis and granted it as part of the same combined motion and roll call.

cases.name: 123 Lafayette Avenue — Off-Street Parking & Backing-Into-Right-of-Way Variance

timeline.summary: Second companion application in the Lafayette Avenue group, seeking a 4-space off-street parking variance and the same backing-into-right-of-way relief for the same solar-panel-driven reasons; granted unanimously as part of the combined motion covering all three properties.

cases.name: 62 Nethermont Avenue — Accessory Apartment Legalization
cases.address: 62 Nethermont Avenue, North White Plains, NY
cases.applicant: 62 Nethermont Avenue Corp / Jim and Luanne Miller

timeline.summary: Applicants sought to legalize a decades-old, previously undocumented accessory apartment, requiring a minimum-dwelling-area variance (327 sq ft provided vs. 800 sq ft required, a 473 sq ft shortfall) and a variance for zero on-site parking spaces (two required); the owners testified the apartment predated their 2010 purchase and that they were adding required parking to resolve a related street-parking complaint. A supportive neighbor and several letters of support were entered into the record. A neighbor from a nearby property (near 5 Grove Road) objected that legalizing the undersized apartment would set a town-wide precedent enabling similar illegal apartments elsewhere, though he did not object to adding the parking itself. The board found the long-existing condition would not change neighborhood character and granted both variances unanimously.

cases.name: Wayne Valley Road — Garage Addition Side Yard Variance
cases.address: 3 Wayne Valley Road, Armonk, NY (ASR renders the applicant name unclear)

timeline.summary: A young family, recent homebuyers, sought a roughly 4-foot side yard setback variance (25 feet required, ~21 feet provided) to widen a narrow existing garage, having consulted with the affected neighbor who raised no objection. The board found no notices or objections, a non-substantial variance, and granted it unanimously.

cases.name: 11 Troy Lane — Shed Legalization Side Yard Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought to legalize a roughly 12-to-20-year-old shed on an existing concrete slab, discovered during an unrelated fence permit inspection, requiring a 5-foot side yard setback variance (15 feet required, 10 feet provided). Moving the shed to comply would require extending the concrete slab and removing mature plantings. The board found the long-standing, unopposed condition non-substantial and granted the variance unanimously.

cases.name: 2 Middle Patent Road — Barn-to-Residence Conversion Variance

timeline.summary: Applicants sought to convert an existing barn/storage building (within its current footprint) into a two-bedroom residence for family use, requiring side yard setback variances of 24.6 feet for the barn structure and 27.2 feet for a new covered entry (30 feet required in each case). A long-time neighbor across the road testified at length in support of the property's rural/historic character but raised detailed concerns about construction-truck traffic on narrow Middle Patent Road (citing an unrelated ongoing pool project on the same larger property), drainage/runoff near her property, and asked the applicants to use the property's other, state-road driveway for construction access where possible; she was not opposed to the variance itself. The board found the setback variances, while numerically substantial as a percentage, would not be visible from the road or change neighborhood character, and granted both unanimously.

cases.name: Armonk Office/Warehouse — Combined Use Parking Variance
cases.address: Tax parcel 107.04, Block 2, Lot 22, Armonk, NY (RELIP district; street address garbled in ASR)
cases.applicant: Property owner Elizabeth Weiss / Herma Realty, on behalf of an incoming tenant (an apparel/embroidery company; company name unclear from ASR)

timeline.summary: The existing office/warehouse building has only 35 on-site parking spaces, but the town code's combined office/warehouse/light-manufacturing parking formula for the incoming tenant's proposed use required 88, necessitating a 53-space variance. The tenant's principals testified the operation would have at most 35-40 total employees (roughly 15-25 warehouse staff, many of whom carpool or are dropped off, plus about 15 office staff) with no retail or walk-in customer traffic, and that the existing lot had historically been adequate for similar prior office/warehouse tenants. Board members pressed on whether the code's per-square-foot calculation for the small embroidery/light-manufacturing component overstated actual parking demand, whether any conditions could cap headcount, and what would happen if the lot proved insufficient; the applicant's attorney and the tenant stated they would seek off-site leased parking rather than allow street parking if that occurred. The board found the variance would not adversely affect the neighborhood, granted it conditioned on Planning Board site plan approval, and tied it to the specific proposed use so that any future different use or expansion would require a new site plan and variance review.

cases.name: 655 Bedford Road (Lindman) — Two-Lot Subdivision Frontage Variance
cases.applicant: Evan and Debron Lindman (subdivision applicant; represented by contractor's attorney Tony Veneziano)

timeline.summary: Applicant sought relief under NY Town Law Section 280-a(3) from the 150-foot public-road-frontage requirement for a two-lot subdivision of a roughly 20-73-acre parcel, proposing to access the single new house via a private easement/driveway off an existing cul-de-sac rather than public frontage. The larger plan (part of a related multi-lot conservation layout) is to build one house and permanently donate the other four potential building lots (about 14 acres) to the town as a conservation easement/fee donation. A neighboring cul-de-sac resident questioned the house's exact siting, the nature of the access driveway, and construction-period disruption, but was not opposed once he understood only a single home was being built well back from the road. The board found the variance minimal, not self-created in any disqualifying way, and a net environmental positive given the conservation donation, and granted it unanimously.

cases.name: 21 Calvary/Cobble Park Drive (Conyers Farm) — Farm Animal Number Variance
cases.address: 21 Calvary Park Drive, Armonk, NY (Conyers Farm)
cases.applicant: Fifth Avenue Properties, LLC (owner/resident Christie Clark)

timeline.summary: Following a neighbor complaint and a building department notice of violation, the applicant sought a variance to keep more animals than the base zoning allows on a roughly 10.5-acre Conyers Farm parcel (part of a larger ~33-acre commonly-owned holding with a 10-acre-minimum private covenant): 30 poultry and 13 other animals (7 goats, 2 donkeys, 4 sheep) against a code maximum of 12 poultry and 4 other animals, a variance of 18 chickens and 9 other animals. The applicant's attorney presented detailed animal-husbandry practices (feeding, veterinary care, waste disposal, enclosed paddocks, no grazing) and noted the animals predated current ownership and are kept for personal/pet use, not breeding or commercial farming; goats were separately already permitted under a 1999 certificate of occupancy. Board members, concerned the variance would run with the land to a future owner who might not maintain the same care practices, negotiated with the applicant's attorney to fix the exact number and species of animals, prohibit breeding and roosters, require animals to stay confined to the existing barn/paddock structures shown on the site survey (with any building changes requiring new approval), and add a Building Inspector compliance inspection every three years (modeled on the town's horse-barn special permit practice). The board adopted an unlisted-action/no-significant-impact SEQRA determination and granted the variance unanimously with these conditions.

cases.name: Frank Residence — Gross Land Coverage Variance
cases.address: 3 [street name garbled in ASR, rendered "Yearage Lane"], Armonk, NY

timeline.summary: For a roughly 2.3-acre R2A property with a home under construction, the applicant sought a gross land coverage variance of 1,146 sq ft (about 8% over the 14,039.3 sq ft maximum), driven by driveway, paver, and below-grade coverage rather than any increase in house size or setback encroachment; the applicant noted grass pavers received a 50% coverage credit and cited a drainage retention basin and culvert system addressing runoff concerns. Five neighbors submitted letters of support, while three neighboring letters objected — but on grounds of the house's overall size/appearance and anticipated noise/quality-of-life concerns rather than the lot-coverage variance itself. The board found the objections did not address the actual criterion before it, found the variance small (under 10%) and not substantial, and granted it unanimously.

cases.name: 17 Orchard Drive (Boyd) — Shed Rear Yard Setback Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought an 11-foot rear yard setback variance (15 feet required, 4 feet provided) to place a 10x16 storage shed on the flattest usable portion of his rear yard, matching the placement of similar accessory structures on neighboring properties along the same rear property line. Directly abutting neighbors, present and by prior conversation, supported the placement. The board acknowledged the variance was numerically substantial relative to the setback but found the practical yard-usability rationale and lack of any objection outweighed that, and granted it unanimously.

cases.name: 1 Leisure Farm Drive (Weiss) — Carport Gross Land Coverage Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 2,779 sq ft gross land coverage variance (about 27% over the 10,046 sq ft maximum) to allow an existing ~20-year-old carport to remain, explaining that removing it (the code-compliant alternative) would leave the house without safe winter access to the front door due to driveway icing. No neighbors objected. The board found the variance numerically substantial but mitigated by the carport's long, unobjected-to existence and the impracticality of the removal alternative, and granted it unanimously.

cases.name: North Castle Drive Hotel (Mad by Dawn Armonk LLC) — Additional Story Variance

timeline.summary: As part of a larger 32-acre mixed-use development (roughly 10.68 acres of hotel zoned OBH and 21 acres of townhouse development under a 2018 rezoning), the applicant sought a variance to build a four-story, 124-key, ~82,000 sq ft hotel where the OBH zone permits a maximum of three stories, after market feedback from prospective hotel operators indicated a three-story design was not viable. The building height itself would remain unchanged at the code-maximum 45 feet regardless of story count. The Town Board had already authorized amending the project's environmental findings statement (scheduled for adoption December 14) to reflect four stories at 45 feet, and the Planning Board had issued a positive referral recommending the ZBA grant the variance. With only three members present, the Town Attorney flagged the applicant's right to an adjournment given the narrow panel, but the applicant elected to proceed; the board found the story-count increase substantial in isolation but mitigated by the unchanged 45-foot height cap, no feasible alternative given the market findings, no negative input from residents, and a favorable environmental review, and granted the variance unanimously.

cases.name: Sniffen Road — Pool/Patio Gross Land Coverage Variance
cases.applicant: Applicant represented by architect Chris Broda

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 3,667.62 sq ft gross land coverage variance (about 31% over the 11,630.77 sq ft maximum) to construct an in-ground pool, expand an existing patio, add a basketball play area away from the driveway, and relocate a barbecue currently sited too close to the septic system into compliance. The house already exceeded coverage limits before any new work, and site constraints (rock outcropping, septic leach field, setbacks) confined the project to a narrow buildable area at the rear of the property, screened from neighbors by topography and vegetation. No neighbors objected. The board found the variance substantial in percentage but mitigated by the site's unique constraints and lack of any feasible alternative, and granted it unanimously.

cases.name: 33 Woodland Road — Front-Yard Pool Lot-Size Variance
cases.address: 33 Woodland Road, Bedford, NY (property within North Castle)
cases.applicant: Property owner represented by landscape architect Dean Pushler

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a large variance (3.831 acres) from the town code's requirement that a lot be at least three times the minimum lot size (6 acres required; the lot is 2.169 acres) before a pool can be sited in what the code classifies as a front yard. Due to the property's unusual shape, a long driveway approaching from what is technically the front but functions practically as the back of the house (with the true rear yard consumed by wetlands, a pond, septic reserve area, and rock ledge), the only feasible pool location fell on the code-defined "front yard" side. Board members debated at length whether the site's cul-de-sac/driveway configuration should change which side counted as the front yard, ultimately leaving that determination to the building inspector, and expressed continued discomfort with the size of the variance. No neighbors objected, and the Planning Board had issued a positive referral. The variance passed 3-1, with one abstention.

cases.name: 100 Business Park Drive (Basis Industrial Acquisition LLC) — Self-Storage Warehouse FAR & Parking Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought to amend a previously-approved second warehouse building on an 11.27-acre PLI-zoned site to add three internal stories of self-storage within the same building footprint, requiring an FAR variance (0.43 proposed vs. 0.3 maximum, a 0.13/~43% increase) and a parking variance (220 spaces provided vs. 277 required, a 57-space shortfall), with the applicant offering to bind the FAR variance to self-storage use only via a developer's agreement. Multiple business park neighbors, represented by attorney Daria/David Chefetz-Isaiah and several property owners (including the park's original developer), submitted detailed written and oral opposition arguing self-storage is not a permitted use in the PLI zone at all, that the building's placement destroys buffer trees and crowds an adjacent property, that the FAR increase would set a precedent other business park owners could invoke, and that existing outdoor storage/construction-yard activity on the site already violates its permits. Because several late-arriving opposition submissions had not been reviewed by the board or applicant's counsel, the board closed the public hearing but tabled its decision, setting a January 19 deadline for both sides to submit final written responses and continuing the matter to the February 2, 2023 meeting; the Town Attorney also flagged legal/use-interpretation issues that might warrant executive session discussion.

cases.name: 10 New King Street — Fence Height Variance
cases.address: 10 New King Street, White Plains, NY

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 2-foot fence-height variance (existing/proposed 8 feet vs. the 6-foot code maximum) to extend a screening fence around an industrial storage yard by roughly 50 feet. The board found the request a minimal, non-substantial extension of an already-nonconforming condition with no evidence of adverse impact on neighboring properties, and granted it.

cases.name: 901 North Broadway — Church Lot Coverage Variance

timeline.summary: A congregation sought a large lot-coverage variance (site at roughly 99.6% coverage against a 50% code maximum) tied to a Town Board special-use-permit referral to occupy an existing commercial building as a church. Representatives described a single weekly Sunday service, occasional counseling use, and minimal traffic impact given carpooling and existing large rear parking. No neighbors objected or submitted comments, and the board found no adverse neighborhood or environmental impact, granting the variance.

cases.name: 10 Starkey Road — Deck Setback Variance

timeline.summary: Applicants sought side-yard (8.7 ft) and rear-yard (12.5 ft) setback variances to replace and connect two existing decks, one of which had been damaged when a neighbor's tree branch fell on it. A neighboring property owner submitted a letter objecting on the belief the addition would encroach closer to their line; after discussion the board and applicant's representative clarified the new deck would actually sit farther from that property, not closer. The board granted the variance on condition that the surface remain flat with only a code-required safety railing, no other vertical additions.

cases.name: 36 Main Street — Gas Station Legalization & Storage Sheds
cases.applicant: Property owner represented by counsel (existing gas station/service site)

timeline.summary: A longtime Main Street gas station sought to legalize decades-old nonconforming conditions — a canopy over a rear oil tank set back only 4.3 feet where 30 feet is required, and fuel pumps set back 9.1 feet where 15 feet is required — as part of a planning-board-referred site plan adding three new, zoning-compliant vertical storage sheds behind the building. The board found the pumps and canopy had existed unchanged in the same positions for roughly 25 years without incident, that nothing new was being added in those nonconforming areas, and granted both variances.

cases.name: Equestrian Estate (21.62-Acre Former Horse Farm) — Multiple Area Variances
cases.applicant: Chloe [surname unclear per ASR, rendered as "McEl-"]

timeline.summary: Applicant sought several area variances (accessory-building size exceeding 25% of the principal building, paddock/property-line setback, and wetland-control-area setback) to redevelop a 21.62-acre former horse farm (R4 zone) with a new residence, a renovated (and actually reduced-in-size) indoor riding arena, a stable, and a garage with grooms' quarters, to board up to 20 horses matching the number just authorized in the Town Board's special permit. A neighboring family (the Geises) wrote in supportive of the project but asking for assurances on a 150-foot buffer and future screening; the applicant agreed to accommodate that as a condition. The Board found the variances individually substantial but mitigated by the property's long equestrian history, extensive prior review by the ARB, Conservation Board, Planning Board and Town Board, and lack of any shown negative environmental or neighbor impact, and granted all variances unanimously, conditioned on no commercial use of the horses and adherence to commitments made to neighbors.

cases.name: Susan Benthol — 22 Starkey Road — Deck Legalization Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 12.19-foot side-yard setback variance to legalize an existing deck (built over a 30-year-old patio) as part of resolving outstanding certificates of occupancy for a two-lot, non-conforming property. The deck had already been reduced in size to comply with impervious-surface limits. No neighbors appeared or objected. The Board found the variance substantial on paper but mitigated by the deck's 30-year history and lack of any feasible alternative, and granted it unanimously.

cases.name: Herblue Realty LLC — Emergency Generator Front-Yard Setback Variance

timeline.summary: Owner of a 5.3-acre warehouse building (recently approved by the Planning Board for a golf-apparel tenant) sought a 151.8-foot front-yard setback variance to install a generator required to power the building's fire pump, which is fed by an on-site pond rather than public water. The applicant's engineer testified that alternative locations (rear of building or inside) would cost roughly $500,000 more due to steep rock ledge and conduit runs. The Board found the variance substantial but justified by significant economic hardship, safety necessity (fire-pump power), and lack of any neighbor complaint, granting it 3-1.

cases.name: Joseph and Celeste Raul — 209 Bedford Banksville Road — Multiple Site Plan Variances

timeline.summary: On referral from the Planning Board, applicants sought eight variances (gross floor area, gross land coverage, accessory-structure size and height, and accessory-apartment provisions) to expand existing accessory structures (stable, garage, pool house) on a 6.03-acre flag-lot parcel that is part of a legally subdivided 1993 five-lot subdivision. As a mitigating condition, the applicant agreed to deed-restrict an adjoining 4-acre parcel in perpetuity to agricultural/horticultural use only, effectively merging it into an 11-acre holding. The Board found the variances numerous and substantial but mitigated by the deed restriction, the Planning Board's favorable view, and lack of any changed use, granting them unanimously.

cases.name: James Dempsey — Cameron Road — Barn/Accessory-Apartment Interpretation & Area Variances

timeline.summary: Applicant first asked the Board to overturn the Building Inspector's determination that a roughly 300-year-old barn (long used as an accessory apartment) had been fully demolished and rebuilt as a 'new' structure rather than a pre-1984 pre-existing non-conforming building, which would avoid triggering area-variance requirements. Neighbors testified the original structure was completely removed down to a pile of rubble and rebuilt with new materials; the applicant's contractor and counsel argued significant original material was salvaged and reused, and the Historical Society's president cited precedent for similar rebuild-in-place projects retaining historic character. The Board denied the interpretation challenge 3-1, deferring to the Building Inspector's determination that this is legally a new structure. It then separately granted the three area variances needed to rebuild the accessory apartment in the same footprint and size as before, unanimously, finding no negative impact and noting the apartment use itself was not in dispute.

cases.name: Jonathan Levine and Amy Wasserman — 5 Sunrise Place — Front Porch Variance

timeline.summary: Applicants sought a 6-foot front-yard setback variance (44 ft provided vs. 50 ft required) to replace a crumbling front porch and expand it into a more usable outdoor space for their children. No neighbors objected or commented. The Board found the variance a fairly diminished (about 12%) ask that would improve rather than harm the neighborhood's character, with no environmental impact, and granted it unanimously.

cases.name: Freedom Road Residence — Front Vestibule Addition Variance
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by Jonathan Milani, design consultant)

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 2.23-foot front-yard setback variance (27.77 ft provided vs. 30 ft required) for a new front vestibule added to a two-story addition. The variance arose because a modular home component arrived with its structural beam offset from where the architect's plans specified, forcing the staircase and vestibule closer to the front of the house than intended. The homeowner, who grew up on the street, reported no neighbor objections. The Board found the roughly 2-foot, under-10% variance de minimis, self-created only incidentally (a modular-construction mismatch), and granted it unanimously.

cases.name: 868 North Broadway LLC — Retail Building Front Yard & Parking Variance Renewal

timeline.summary: Applicant sought to renew front-yard (0.5 ft provided vs. 10 ft required) and off-street parking (13 vs. 22 required) variances originally granted in April 2019 but which had since expired after a decade-long effort to secure building permits (delayed by engineering issues and a lost prospective tenant). Counsel represented the plans were unchanged from the prior approval. No public comment was received. The Board found the same findings from the original 2019 grant applied and granted the renewal unanimously.

cases.name: Hot Blow Dry Salon — 450 Main Street — Parking Variance

timeline.summary: A growing local blow-dry salon sought a 13-space parking variance (160 provided vs. 173 required) to relocate into a larger space in the CVS-anchored shopping center, since salon uses require more parking per code than the prior retail use. A parking study over several weekdays showed the lot never exceeded half its capacity. No neighbors or tenants raised concerns. The Board found the shortfall diminimus relative to the 173-space total and driven by the statute's classification rather than any real parking problem, granting it unanimously.

cases.name: 45 Bedford Road LLC — Townhouse Development Coverage & FAR Variances

timeline.summary: For a 34-townhouse project on 4.3 acres (already granted a Town Board special permit), the applicant sought a 3.7% building-coverage variance and a 0.077 FAR variance, both stemming from Town Board and Planning Board requests during the special-permit process: buildings along Bedford Road were lowered and spread out to respond to concerns from the adjacent 1848 historic district, and previously-open underground parking was enclosed at the Planning Board's request, which pushed FAR over the limit. Both the Planning Board and Town Board had already endorsed these exact changes in the special-permit findings. The Board found the variances not substantial in context, self-created only in the sense of complying with the other boards' own requests, and granted them unanimously; the project still requires Planning Board site-plan approval.

cases.name: Greenwich Realty Group LLC — Bedford Banksville Road — Self-Storage Warehouse Height Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant, who had already cleaned up a prior nonconforming trucking/fill operation on the site (evicting tenants and paying a $20,000 building-department fine), sought a variance to build a three-story self-storage building where two stories are the maximum permitted, replacing a condemned building that the building department had ordered removed. The building's height (30 ft) would not change, only the number of floors; septic capacity limits occupancy to roughly 16-20 people, keeping the self-storage use low-traffic. The Board found the variance not substantial given the unchanged height and low-intensity use, and granted it unanimously; the project still requires Planning Board site-plan approval.

cases.name: Robert D. Silvestry — 19 Maryland Avenue — Porch Enclosure Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought front-yard (23.75 ft) and side-yard (12.25 ft) setback variances to enclose an existing, already non-conforming entry porch as a small mudroom for family/dog convenience, without expanding the existing footprint. No neighbor encroachment or objection was noted. The Board found the variance substantial in percentage terms but mitigated by the fact that the applicant was merely enclosing (not enlarging) an existing non-conforming footprint, with no feasible alternative, and granted it unanimously, with a condition limiting the relief to the porch area only.

cases.name: Joel Beltran — 22 General Heath Avenue — Rear Deck Side Yard Variance
cases.address: 22 General Heath Avenue, North White Plains, NY

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 3.7-foot combined side-yard setback variance to place new decking material over an existing raised slab in the rear yard of an already non-conforming property; no closer encroachment to the side yard than the existing (non-conforming) residence itself. No neighbors appeared or objected. The Board found the variance minor (about 3.5 feet), with the only alternative being to leave the slab uncovered, and granted it unanimously.

cases.name: Brian and Amy Towers — Generator Replacement Side Yard Variance

timeline.summary: Applicants sought an 8.1-foot side-yard setback variance to replace an existing, smaller non-conforming generator with a larger 80kW unit needed to run a geothermal heating system, sited roughly 18 feet from the old unit's location due to steep grade nearby. Board members confirmed the adjacent propane tanks (not being relocated) were themselves conforming, avoiding any need for additional relief. The Board found the variance modest (about 16%) and justified by the need to run continuous geothermal pumps, granting it unanimously.

cases.name: Alizandro (Alex) and Daniela Meda — 298 Bedford Banksville Road — Gross Land Coverage Variance

timeline.summary: Applicants, who purchased a deteriorated ~4-acre hilltop property, sought a large (roughly 38-39%) gross-land-coverage variance to rebuild/expand the house (adding about 1,193 sq ft), add a three-car garage with an attic playroom, and convert the existing garage to an office, while a preexisting driveway and tennis court already accounted for about 64% of total coverage before any new construction. A downhill neighbor (whose family had lived there decades) raised concerns about existing stormwater runoff reaching her house/basement and asked whether the proposed mitigation system would address the full variance amount, not just the incremental increase; the applicant's designer and the building department representative described a robust stormwater-capture system (exceeding code minimums by roughly 10x) subject to town engineer review. The Board conditioned the grant on no accessory apartment/additional living space and no unrelated construction-business trucking, finding the coverage issue driven mainly by the preexisting driveway/tennis court and the stormwater plan an improvement over existing conditions, and granted it unanimously.

cases.name: Daniel Grobman — 7 Spruce Hill Road — Storage Shed Side Yard Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 0.2-foot side-yard setback variance to convert a decades-old storage shed (unchanged footprint) into a home office, insulating it and adding a ductless heating/cooling split; a routine residential-project-review survey had found the shed two inches closer to the neighbor's line than code allows. No questions or objections arose, and the Board granted the variance unanimously, remarking it was likely the smallest variance ever considered by the Board.

cases.name: Marquis Associates LLC — 56 Lafayette Avenue — Film/TV Studio Conversion Parking Variance
cases.address: 56 Lafayette Avenue, North White Plains, NY

timeline.summary: Owner of a 32,000-square-foot, 28%-vacant warehouse building (previously granted a 12-13 space parking variance in 2009) sought to convert 4,100 sq ft of vacant warehouse space to a film/TV/photography studio, which the Town Planner classified as office use for parking purposes, driving the total requirement to 91 spaces against 66 provided. After a pointed dispute between the applicant's attorney and the Board's attorney over whether the new shortfall was 13 spaces (incremental) or 25 spaces (total, since the prior variance would be subsumed into this one), the applicant's attorney conceded the Board's characterization of a 25-space variance. Applicant's team argued film/photography production draws far less parking demand than a typical office (crews often arrive via production-company vans or public transit) and that the building had run at 94% occupancy in the past with parking problems only when an unrelated business improperly let outside customers park there. The Board granted the 25-space variance unanimously, conditioned on the site plan and any future higher-parking-demand tenant changes remaining subject to Planning Board review.

cases.name: 23 Cat Rock Drive — Roslin Garage/Land Coverage Variance

timeline.summary: Applicants sought a gross land coverage variance of 1,124 sq ft (16,730 sq ft permitted, 19,854 sq ft proposed) under Town Code 355-26(C) to construct a new two-story, three-car garage, converting the existing garage into a family room. The board found the ~18% variance justified because it replaces an existing garage with the same number of vehicle spaces, doesn't change the neighborhood character, and drew no neighbor objections. Approved unanimously 3-0.

cases.name: 21 Wampus Lake Drive — Olinow New Dwelling Land Coverage Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a gross land coverage variance of 1,776 sq ft (25,633 sq ft permitted, ~27,409 sq ft proposed) under Town Code 355-26(C) to construct a new one-family dwelling, represented by architect Scott Fisher. The new design rotates the house footprint and shrinks the driveway and tennis-court surround, reducing overall coverage by roughly 3,000 sq ft versus existing conditions even though it remains over the maximum allowable by about 6-7%. No neighbor correspondence or objections were received. Approved unanimously 3-0.

cases.name: William Rothke Addition — Side Yard Setback Variance

timeline.summary: Applicants, represented by Amanda Lynn Hart, sought a side yard setback variance of 7 feet (25 ft required, 18 ft provided) under Town Code 355-21 in an R1A district to add a second garage bay and mudroom as part of a larger addition to an existing 2,800 sq ft split-level house. The added bay does not increase the number of parking spaces and sits on a hillside lower than neighboring properties, with substantial screening/greenery on that side. No neighbor objections were received despite proper notice. Approved unanimously 3-0.

cases.name: 113 Round Hill Road — Patel Fence Height Variance

timeline.summary: In an R2A district, applicant sought to legalize an installed fence with a height variance of 8 inches (6 ft maximum, 6'8" installed) under Town Code 355-15(G). The installer's representative argued the small overage, measured differently depending on grade, was not substantial, and the board noted supportive letters from neighbors. Approved unanimously.

cases.name: 23 Whippoorwill Road East — Verizon/Kent Place Municipal Parking Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a building coverage variance (15% maximum, 23.49% proposed, roughly 8% over) under Town Code 355-21 to subdivide roughly one acre off its two-acre parcel and convey it to the town to expand the municipal Kent Place parking lot downtown, while relocating and rebuilding Verizon's own parking. A neighbor (Curtis Spagavan, 25 Whippoorwill Road East) raised concerns about existing chronic flooding and wetland encroachment behind his property; the project's consulting engineer described stormwater detention, floodplain mitigation, and streambank regrading planned as part of the associated Planning Board site plan review, which would include a further public hearing on drainage. The Planning Board had already issued a positive referral. Approved unanimously.

cases.name: 9 Sterling Road North — Harris Pool/Deck Land Coverage Variance

timeline.summary: After roughly five and a half years and multiple design iterations before the Planning Board and Conservation Board, applicant sought a gross land coverage variance of 2,574 sq ft under Town Code 355-60.1(F) to construct a 760 sq ft pool and deck in an R2A district, including legalizing an as-built driveway that turned out larger than originally permitted. The hearing was briefly paused when the board received a late planner memo raising new wetland/septic issues; after review, the applicant's representative explained the septic system was relocated to meet current code, the driveway was rebuilt with permeable pavers reducing runoff, and the Conservation Board had accepted the wetland mitigation plan as a net environmental benefit. The board found the roughly 19% variance substantial on its face but justified by the property's pre-existing nonconformity and the applicant's mitigation efforts, and approved subject to Planning Board final site plan approval.

cases.name: 32 Orchard Drive — 12.9-Acre Subdivision Access Variance
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by attorneys Whitney Singleton and Ralph)

timeline.summary: In an R1A district, applicant sought relief under NY Town Law 280-a (and a local analog requiring 25 ft of cul-de-sac frontage, none provided) to subdivide a 12.9-acre parcel into four new lots plus the existing house, with the rear lot accessed via an easement over an existing driveway rather than a fee-title strip that would bisect a neighboring lot and require more tree/slope disturbance. The Planning Board had already issued a favorable referral. A nearby neighbor (Eric Mark, 5 Eden Hunt Place) raised drainage, slope, and screening concerns about the eventual house siting, which the board and applicant's counsel noted was a Planning Board site-plan matter for a later hearing, not before the ZBA that night; counsel offered to share plans directly with him. The board granted the variance conditioned on limiting the property to a maximum of five total residences.

cases.name: 61 Ridge Road — Percal Deck Rebuild Setback Variance

timeline.summary: The Percal application was announced but not heard; it was adjourned to the April meeting because of a notice issue.

cases.name: 86 Byram Ridge Road — Fisher Portico Variance

timeline.summary: In an R1A district, applicants sought a front-yard setback variance of 4.06 feet (50 ft required, 45.94 ft provided) to construct a small decorative portico over the front entry. The board found the variance de minimis, beneficial to the neighborhood character, and with no environmental impact or neighbor objection. Approved unanimously.

cases.name: Gabby's Restaurant (15 Old Route 22) — Mixed-Use FAR and Parking Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought an FAR variance (proposed 0.3769 vs. 0.3 maximum) and an off-street parking variance (6-space deficiency, 50 provided of 56 required) under the town code to demolish a dilapidated accessory building and replace it with a new mixed-use structure containing four residential apartments, ground-floor retail space, and four garage spaces, alongside restaurant renovations (larger ADA-compliant bathrooms, expanded dining room, new rear patio). The board pressed on whether the garage spaces and FAR would be classified as residential versus commercial and on parking alternatives (referencing 8 public parallel spaces across the street). The board found the FAR overage not substantial and the parking deficiency justified by the project's benefits (finishing the streetscape, generating tax revenue), and granted the variance conditioned on the four garage spaces remaining residential-only in perpetuity, the retail space remaining retail use, Planning Board site plan approval, and any future FAR/parking changes returning to the ZBA.

cases.name: 23 Banksville Bedford Road — Readage Reality Corp (Withdrawn)
cases.address: 23 Banksville Bedford Road, North Castle, NY

timeline.summary: The applicant's variance application, originally item four on the agenda, was withdrawn before the meeting and no hearing was held.

cases.name: 61 Ridge Road — Percal Deck Rebuild Setback Variance

timeline.summary: In an R1A district, applicants sought a rear-yard setback variance of 9.25 feet (40 ft required, 30.75 ft provided) under Town Code 355-21 to replace a rotted, unusable deck with a squared-off version sized to fit an outdoor table. Mrs. Percal presented in her husband's absence and submitted a letter of no objection from the adjoining rear neighbor. No other neighbor objections were received. Approved unanimously 3-0.

cases.name: 20 Round Hill Road — Holburn Family Compound Variances

timeline.summary: On a 16-acre parcel (part of a larger 20-acre lot-line realignment before the Planning Board) subject to a 10-acre deeded conservation easement, applicant sought three variances under Town Code for an accessory barn/apartment/greenhouse structure: an accessory-structure height variance of 1'2" (22 ft allowed, 23.2 ft proposed, driven by equipment clearance needs); a variance to allow an accessory apartment in a structure built after 1984; and a variance of the required 4-year (or 2-year-ownership) waiting period before installing an accessory apartment. Represented by attorney Corey Salum, who argued the restrictions no longer serve their original purpose given the regional housing shortage and urged the board not to impose a family-only rental restriction. The board discussed but declined to impose a rental-restriction condition, noted a supportive neighbor letter, and granted all three variances by separate votes, contingent on Planning Board site plan/special permit approval.

cases.name: 7 Niles Avenue — Carport Setback Variance
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by architect Michael Picorello)

timeline.summary: Applicant sought rear-yard and side-yard setback variances (side yard: 9 ft required, 4.9 ft provided) to construct an open, four-post carport near the existing driveway, needed because the property's undersized existing garage cannot be accessed and vehicles otherwise must back the full driveway length onto the street. The property backs up to the fire department, which raised no objection. A board member pressed on visibility and screening toward an adjacent neighbor's house; the architect noted a rendering showed an attractive design and that screening wasn't feasible given the carport's angle. Approved unanimously.

cases.name: 5 Overlook Road — Residential Elevator Setback Variance
cases.applicant: Property owners (represented by architect Michael Picorello)

timeline.summary: On a non-conforming corner lot fronting both Route 22 and Overlook Road (giving it two front-yard setbacks), applicants with health issues sought a 13.5-foot setback variance to install a small residential ('Lula'-type) elevator on the rear corner of a raised-ranch home, the only feasible location, to allow them to age in place without navigating stairs between the garage level and living areas. A next-door neighbor of 36 years spoke in support. The board found the lot's dual-front condition the operative hardship. Approved unanimously.

cases.name: 4 Trip Lane — Driveway Pier Height and Width Variances
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by Michael Cerrano and engineer Rick Bolinger)

timeline.summary: As the final technical step before Planning Board site plan approval following a multi-year code-enforcement history (unpermitted driveway/grading work, pending Justice Court fines), applicant sought a pier-height variance of 1 foot (8 ft permitted, 9 ft with decorative light fixtures) and a driveway-width variance of 6.25 feet (18 ft maximum, 24.25 ft existing) for previously-built driveway improvements on Trip Lane, a road that transitions from residential to a busy school-campus entrance. A board member pressed on potential stormwater runoff impact to an adjacent, newly built but unoccupied house (6 Trip Lane); counsel noted the driveway's grading predates that construction and drains to an underground system reviewed by the town engineer. The board granted both variances conditioned on the Planning Board/town engineer confirming no adverse runoff impact to the neighboring property.

cases.name: 103 Miami River Road — Swansberg/Menacal Front Yard Setback Variance

timeline.summary: In an R4A district, applicants sought a front-yard setback variance of 6'8" (75 ft required, 68'4" existing/proposed) under Town Code 355-21 for renovations to a 1700s-era, pre-existing nonconforming house, with no change to the existing setback and only a 16 sq ft increase in building coverage. The project had already received Architectural Review Board approval. Approved unanimously.

cases.name: 45 Nethermont Avenue — Villain Front Porch/Stairway Variance
cases.address: 45 Nethermont Avenue, North White Plains, NY

timeline.summary: On a corner lot with two front yards (Nethermont Avenue and Roberta Place), applicants sought a front-yard setback variance of 22 feet for a new porch (30 ft required, 8 ft provided) and a 23-foot variance for an adjoining masonry stairway (27 ft required, 4 ft provided) under Town Code 355-21 and 355-15(C), to replace a deteriorated side entry/platform with a porch that reorients what functions as the home's real entrance. A neighbor across the street on Nethermont Avenue questioned which frontage governed the setback calculation but did not oppose the project once the two-front-yard confusion was clarified. The board found the house already existing nonconforming and the change likely to improve the streetscape. Approved unanimously.

cases.name: 2 Banks Farm Road — Lane Second-Floor Addition Rear Yard Variance

timeline.summary: In an R2A district, applicant sought a rear-yard setback variance of 2 feet (30 ft required, 28 ft provided) under Town Code 355-21 to add a second floor over most of an existing ranch house, with the only nonconformity affecting a small corner where an irregular property line juts inward. Represented by architect John Scarlato. Approved unanimously.

cases.name: 12 Bedford Road — Historic House Law Office/Apartment Driveway & Parking Variance
cases.applicant: 12 [Bedford] LLC (property owner, an attorney converting the house to her law office plus a rental apartment)

timeline.summary: In a historic district office (RO) zone, applicant sought a driveway-width variance of 11 feet (20 ft required for office use, 11.5 ft/9 ft under a second-floor overhang existing) under Town Code 355-56(G) and an off-street parking variance of 2 spaces (9 required, 7 provided) under Town Code 355-57, to convert a historic 1800s house — previously a licensed home-occupation surveyor's office — into a small law office in front and a two-bedroom rental apartment in back, without enlarging the footprint. Applicant argued the code's parking formula overcounts an un-enclosable, landmarked open porch. An adjacent commercial-property owner (Michael Ferrari, 16/20 Bedford Road) strongly opposed, arguing the narrow driveway and 8'6" overhead clearance would violate NY State building/fire code (citing a 9'3" standard ambulance height) and that the ZBA lacked authority to grant a variance conflicting with state code; he offered to negotiate a shared easement instead. The town attorney confirmed the board's authority is limited to town code (state code and historic-registry questions fall to the building inspector), and the building inspector stated the state code items were a separate, later matter for his office. After extensive debate about parking demand, apartment occupancy, and whether the applicant could add one more space, the board kept the public hearing open and adjourned the application to the following month.

cases.name: 20 Overlook Road — Deck Setback Variances (Barone)

timeline.summary: An out-of-state contractor built a roughly 20x20 deck without permits or zoning review, encroaching 4.5 feet into the required front-yard setback and 8.5 feet into the side-yard setback on a steeply sloped, roughly one-third-acre lot. The applicant's representative argued the site's topography and mature trees left no conforming alternative location, and offered privacy plantings to screen the deck from the north neighbor. The board found the front-yard variance minor but the side-yard variance (nearly 50%) substantial, and pressed for written, informed confirmation from the north neighbor (who had only given verbal assent) before approving. The board voted to approve the variance conditioned on that neighbor letter being submitted by August 1, and directed that the contractor be told to obtain a building permit before further work.

cases.name: 486 Bedford Road — St. Nersess Armenian Seminary Married Students' Building Addition

timeline.summary: The seminary sought a side-yard setback variance (30 feet provided vs. 100 feet required, since the required setback for a religious use is double the residential front-yard setback) to add two guest rooms and a residence for the retiring dean onto the existing married-students' building. The applicant's architect noted the addition would sit farther from the property line than the existing nonconforming building, was clustered near existing utilities to avoid disturbing a large green and a septic-constrained area, and was 280 feet from the nearest neighbor (the Green family) with substantial tree screening. The board raised the coverage/FAR numbers (well under the maximums) and suggested, without making it a formal condition, that the applicant obtain a letter from the Green family confirming no objection given their past concerns about screening and occupancy from the original approval.

cases.name: 11 Maryland Avenue — Front/Side Setback and Land Coverage Variances
cases.applicant: Property owner (first name "Wendy"; surname unclear in ASR audio), represented by architect Patrick Croak

timeline.summary: The applicant sought four variances (front yard, two side yards, and gross land coverage) for a small addition to an existing nonconforming home on a sub-standard lot originally subdivided during a 1960s-era sewer project. Discussion focused on confusion over whether the newly requested setbacks were larger or smaller than variances granted for the same house in 2021; the architect clarified the differences were the result of measurement errors on an old survey used for the prior application, not any new encroachment, and that the addition itself does not extend the existing nonconforming walls. The board approved the variances after confirming nothing new was being built closer to the property lines than what already exists.

cases.name: 99 East Middle Patent Road — Mianus River Gorge Equipment Barn

timeline.summary: The land trust sought a variance to build a 936-square-foot post-and-beam equipment barn on a 4.2-acre parcel, exceeding the accessory-structure size cap (25% of the main dwelling) because the existing house is small and nonconforming at only about 1,000 square feet. The barn would consolidate equipment and vehicles (tractor, UTV, trailer) currently scattered across seven storage locations and would also support the organization's deer management program. The applicant noted the barn would be visible only to one neighbor, who had no objection, sits lower than the house, and is well below applicable lot-coverage limits on the surrounding 200+ acre preserve. The board found the variance substantial only because of the small existing house, saw no environmental impact, and approved unanimously.

cases.name: 1 Overlook Road — Deck Rebuild Setback Variance (Rossi)

timeline.summary: The applicant sought to demolish and rebuild a deteriorating deck in essentially the same footprint (squaring off rounded corners, adding about 48 square feet), maintaining the same nonconforming setbacks that had existed since a 1986 permit. All neighbors present voiced support, no board member raised objections, and the board found no change in neighborhood character, no environmental impact, and approved unanimously.

cases.name: 298 Bedford Banksville Road — Accessory Apartment Legalization (Amita)

timeline.summary: The applicant sought to legalize a detached accessory apartment over a garage that had previously been approved only as an office. The board and its attorney determined that a coverage variance the same board granted for this property roughly six months earlier was expressly conditioned on there being no accessory apartment on the site, and that the board could not simply reverse that condition for this new application. The applicant said he had been unaware of that condition and was advised to consult his own attorney about possible paths forward (such as reducing the house's coverage); no variance was granted and the applicant did not press for a vote, effectively leaving the application withdrawn without prejudice.

cases.name: 568-570 Bedford Road — Summit Club at Armonk Parking Credit Variance

timeline.summary: In connection with a new golf-course maintenance facility, the planning board determined the overall golf-course-community floating overlay district (residences, clubhouse, amenities) was about 61 parking spaces short when calculated as a single district. The applicant requested a 65-space parking variance/credit, reasoning that residents of the community's 65 market-rate units are required to be golf-club members but would walk or use golf carts rather than drive to the clubhouse, and that no parking would ever be permitted off-site (a condition of the related Town Board special permit). The board found the logic reasonable and approved unanimously.

cases.name: 12 Bedford Road — Office/Residence Driveway Width & Parking Variance
cases.applicant: Property owner/attorney at 12 Bedford Road (name not clearly captured in the ASR audio)

timeline.summary: Carried over from the July meeting, this case sought a driveway-width variance (about 11.5 feet short of the required 20 feet) and a one-space parking variance for a mixed residential/home-office use in a historic house with a non-enclosable landmarked porch. A neighboring commercial-property owner, Robert Ferrari, opposed the application on fire-safety and shared-driveway-alternative grounds; the applicant rebutted at length, presenting statements from the fire commissioner and a prior owner that driveway width was never an operational issue, and objected to being pressured into a shared easement with Ferrari. The board's attorney found the fire-code argument outside the board's zoning purview and declined to require lease disclosures about the substandard driveway. The board approved both variances unanimously.

cases.name: Maraski Taverna — Shopping Center Parking Variance
cases.address: Shopping center on Bedford Road/Cox Lane area, Armonk (exact suite address not clearly captured in the ASR audio)
cases.applicant: Maraski Taverna (owners Chris Longo and Mike Soriese)
