timeline.summary: The restaurant, in business three years, sought to expand into an adjacent long-vacant retail space for additional seating and a bar, requiring a 15-space parking variance for the shopping center as a whole. The applicant presented a week-long parking utilization study (counts every two hours) showing the lot never exceeded about 42% capacity even accounting for full occupancy of a newer tenant, and that Maraski's peak hours (dinner) do not overlap with the pharmacy or other retail tenants' hours. A board member noted that, practically, ordinary retail use of the same space would already require some parking, so the incremental ask was smaller than the stated 15 spaces; the center also retains 25 land-banked spaces. The board approved unanimously.

cases.name: 84 Byram Ridge Road — Detached Garage Side Yard Variance (Sniffen)

timeline.summary: The applicants sought a 20-foot side-yard variance (5 feet provided vs. 25 required) to build a detached three-car garage across the driveway from their house, sited there because of steep topography, an existing pool/gardens, and septic infrastructure limiting alternatives. The garage would sit only 5 feet from a private road owned by one neighbor (who also maintains it with two other homeowners); that neighbor submitted a supportive letter conditioned on tree screening being maintained/replaced. The board pressed on how such a private, informal condition could be enforced long after the current owners might sell, and ultimately wrote the tree-maintenance and like-kind replacement terms (minimum 8 feet tall) directly into the variance resolution as an enforceable condition, then approved.

cases.name: 14 Middle Patent Road — Horse Farm Barn FAR Variance

timeline.summary: Following the Town Board's recent approval to increase the property's permitted horse count from 10 to 26, the applicant needed floor-area-ratio variances to expand the existing barn (78% over the 25% cap) and build a new second barn (24.3% over the cap), arguing it is essentially impossible to house that many horses under a ratio keyed to the size of the main residence. Counsel noted a nearly identical variance was granted for the same property in 2009. A neighbor across the road raised concerns about visual mass and asked why this wasn't addressed earlier in the process; the applicant's team responded that the FAR variance became necessary only after the planning board's approval imposed the ratio condition, and that no shows, public use, or lessons would occur on the property under the special permit. The board found the size and horse count already vetted by the planning/town boards, deemed the FAR variance a mathematical formality, and approved.

cases.name: 448 Bedford Road — Little Sparrows Nursery School Playground Area Variance
cases.applicant: Hillside Church of the Christian Missionary Alliance / Little Sparrows Nursery School

timeline.summary: A routine interior-repair permit application revealed the 41-year-old nursery school had long operated six classrooms (87 students) under a special-use permit that only authorized two, since amended and unanimously approved by the Town Board; that process in turn surfaced a play-area code requirement (200 square feet per child, applied to full enrollment) that would require 17,400 square feet where only 800 square feet exists. The board found the literal per-child calculation impractical given staggered outdoor schedules that never put more than about 15 children outside at once, and, rather than requiring an unbuildable play-area expansion, approved the variance conditioned on the school never having more than 15 children on the playground at one time. No neighbors objected; the North Castle Historical Society wrote in support.

cases.name: 124 Old Mount Kisco Road — Two-Lot Subdivision Variances (Madonna)

timeline.summary: The applicant sought renewal of nine lot-area, frontage, lot-width, setback, and buildable-area variances needed to subdivide a lot containing one existing home and one fire-damaged home into two conforming lots, essentially identical to variances the same board granted in 2021 that had since expired because the town code has no mechanism to extend variances. Minor changes from the 2021 figures stemmed from a surveyor's correction of legal-description discrepancies with the two adjoining parcels. A neighbor at the adjoining property confirmed he had no objection provided the existing house near his property line does not change size or setback, which the applicant confirmed. The board approved all nine variances unanimously after closing the public hearing.

cases.name: 5 Maryland Avenue — Second-Story Addition Variance
cases.applicant: Melinda Lee Chardello and Vincent Chardello (architect Frank Tancretti)

timeline.summary: Applicants sought side- and front-yard setback variances to add a second story and a small front porch to an existing one-story, two-bedroom home on a narrow 50-foot lot, keeping the home at two bedrooms per a Health Department septic constraint. The board found the variance largely a function of pre-existing nonconformity (narrow lot, existing side yards under the 25-foot code minimum) rather than anything new being created, noted no neighbor objections, and confirmed minimal excavation/environmental impact. The board voted 5-0 to approve.

cases.name: 8 Roseanne Drive — Fence, Accessory Structure & Accessory Apartment Variances

timeline.summary: On a roughly 18-acre estate, the applicant sought a 7-foot variance for a 13-foot fence around a tennis/paddle court complex, a 10.85% variance to build a 3,000-sq-ft accessory structure (limit is 25% of the principal dwelling), and an 11-month variance to allow an accessory apartment for a nanny before the standard two-year post-purchase waiting period elapsed. Board members raised outdoor-lighting concerns (deferred to the planning board, which had hired a lighting consultant) and pressed counsel on whether the family would commit to not renting the apartment to a third party; counsel could not commit but argued the property's high value and family-compound character made transient rental unlikely. The transcript ends mid-deliberation on the five findings without a recorded vote.

cases.name: 6 Sixes Lane — Side Yard Variance for Garage Widening

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 5-foot side-yard variance to widen an existing single-car garage (partly to work around a chimney encroachment) as part of a second-floor addition and new front porch. Two supportive letters from affected neighbors, including a neighboring builder, were submitted, and no neighbors appeared to object. The board approved unanimously on a 3-0 roll call (Ed Lashins, Ray Rodriguez, Robert Greer).

cases.name: 26 Carolyn Place — Land Coverage Variance (Pool/Terrace Reconfiguration)
cases.applicant: Property owner represented by Kory Salomone (Zarin & Steinmetz); project architect Lucio Leo, engineer Ralph Alfonzario

timeline.summary: The applicant, who had purchased the property already over its approved land coverage and then added an unpermitted terrace, proposed removing the illegal terrace and relocating the pool further from the property line and toward the rear, resulting in a net coverage reduction of roughly 4,171 sq ft even though the site would remain about 5,000-6,400 sq ft over the code maximum (accounts differed between the applicant's and planning department's figures). Several board members were troubled that approving the request would effectively legitimize prior unpermitted construction and asked pointed questions about drainage, aquifer/well impact, and septic location, ultimately satisfied that the town engineer and planning board would review those issues at final site plan approval. The board voted 3-0 (Ed Lashins, Ray Rodriguez, Robert Greer) to approve.

cases.name: 700 Bedford Road — Front Yard Setback Variance (Carriage House Rebuild)
cases.applicant: Joe Cassiotis, represented by Shane Baddali

timeline.summary: The applicant sought a front-yard setback variance to rebuild and expand a circa-1850 farmhouse (framed by the applicant as an "addition" to an existing structure) plus a new attached carriage house/breezeway, maintaining the original front wall location for historical streetscape reasons. Board members objected that the original framing had already been completely demolished (following storm damage) before the application was filed, arguing the project should have been treated as new construction rather than an addition to an existing nonconforming structure, and one member said the framing felt like it was presented "under false pretenses," though the applicant's representative said this was unintentional and reflected building-department guidance on how to categorize the filing. The board ultimately voted 4-1 to approve, with Ed Lashins dissenting.

cases.name: 111 Lafayette Avenue — Parking Backing-Out Variance
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented at hearing, applicant/attorney name not clearly captured)

timeline.summary: A minor, uncontested variance from the town code requiring vehicles to pull forward rather than back out onto the street across a sidewalk, for a reconfigured rear parking area with no changes to the building itself. The board found no substantive issues and approved unanimously (5-0).

cases.name: 1551 Old Orchard Street — Deck Legalization Variance

timeline.summary: The current owner sought side-yard, rear-yard, and land-coverage variances to legalize an existing wood deck built by a previous owner before he purchased the property in 2023. The board walked through its standard five-factor test, found no environmental or character impact, and noted the only alternative (demolition) was undesirable; no neighbors appeared. Approved unanimously.

cases.name: 242 Bedford Banksville Road — Entrance Archway Height Variance

timeline.summary: Applicants sought an 8-foot-10-inch variance (proposing 14'10" versus a 6-foot code maximum) to replace an aging stone entrance wall with a tall cedar-and-mahogany archway sized to accommodate emergency vehicles and match the home's modern architectural style. Ed Lashins argued the height was purely aesthetic/a "statement" with no functional necessity, suggesting shorter, more modern pillars could achieve the same emergency-access width without the variance, while other members felt the design was not unusually intrusive for the area (citing similar archways on nearby horse farms) and voted to approve; the board split 2-1 (with a third vote yes), Ed Lashins dissenting.

cases.name: 167 Mianus River Road — Buffer Setback Variances (Mianus River Gorge Preserve)
cases.applicant: Mianus River Gorge Inc. (non-profit land preserve), represented by Rod Cossiam, Executive Director

timeline.summary: The nonprofit sought three related buffer variances (for the building addition, an attached deck, and a generator) to expand its cramped administrative office, citing overcrowding exacerbated by remote work needs and a growing intern/student program. The one directly adjacent landowner submitted a supportive letter; the board found no character or environmental impact given the distance to other neighbors, and approved unanimously.

cases.name: 1613 Old Orchard Street — Driveway Sight-Distance Variance
cases.applicant: Marlene Duran and Diane Rosenberg, represented by attorney Noelle Wolfson and traffic engineer Brian Dempsey (DTS Providence)

timeline.summary: Applicants sought a variance from the code's 200-foot sight-distance requirement (achieving 164 feet without an easement, or approximately 194 feet using an AASHTO stopping-sight-distance standard) to build a driveway for a new single-family home on an otherwise unbuildable vacant lot; the town's own traffic consultant concurred the driveway would have adequate stopping sight distance. Neighbor Frank Aiello strongly objected, citing speeding traffic and safety risk to his grandchildren, and a heated exchange occurred over whether the applicant should compensate him for a sight-distance easement over his property, which the parties had been unable to agree on. The board found the professional traffic analysis persuasive, noted most properties on the street already fall short of the 200-foot standard with no crash history, and voted unanimously to approve despite the neighbor's objection.

cases.name: 2 Meadow Drive — Side/Front Yard Setback Variance (Deck)
cases.applicant: Corey Carlson, represented by Michael Testa

timeline.summary: A corner-lot deck built in 1985 by a previous owner was found to violate a 30-foot minimum side/front-yard setback (providing 25.8 feet) after the current owner, who purchased in 2023 and is now selling, received a building department violation notice. The board found the ~40-year-old deck non-substantial, self-created only by a prior owner, and with no complaint history, and approved unanimously.

cases.name: 157 Mianus River Road — Pool Equipment Pad Setback Variance
cases.applicant: Homeowner Butler, represented by Brian Fiyak (Shoreline Pools)

timeline.summary: Shoreline Pools' representative candidly described the front-yard placement of a pool equipment pad as a "self-inflicted" error, explaining the crew mistook the location for the rear yard and chose a rock-free clearing near an existing utility pole to avoid disturbing tree roots and solid ledge elsewhere on the heavily-rocked, Mianus River Gorge-adjacent lot. The pad, in place roughly a year, is not visible from any neighboring property or the road; the applicant offered to screen it if required. The board approved unanimously.

cases.name: 10 North Lane — Rear Yard Pool, Mechanicals, Shed & Coverage Variances
cases.applicant: Represented by Terrence Carthy on behalf of Pools Perfection (property owner not clearly named)

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 24-foot rear-yard setback variance for a pool (16 feet provided vs. 40 required), plus variances for pool mechanicals, a shed, and a modest land-coverage overage, arguing the irregular lot shape and a steep, wooded slope buffered the site from view. Immediate downhill neighbor Joe Jacobs strongly objected that the hillside would act as an amplifying "amphitheater" for pool and equipment noise into his backyard, and questioned whether alternative, less-intrusive designs had genuinely been explored; board members floated relocating the mechanicals farther from the shared property line and pursuing sound-mitigation options (fencing, plantings) as a possible compromise. No motion could gain support that evening; the board directed the applicant to get a firm construction start date and work informally with the neighbor on mitigation, then adjourned the matter without a vote.

cases.name: 4 Rustling Lane — Fence Height Variance

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 1-foot variance for a 7-foot fence (6-foot code maximum), explaining the fence was purchased at auction before confirming its height was non-conforming and was wanted for security (guard dogs, a cognitively-disabled daughter, delivery traffic). No neighbors objected and other fences on the street were similarly noted; the board approved unanimously, finding the one-foot overage non-substantial.

cases.name: 56/70 Lafayette Avenue — Parking Variance (Warehouse-to-Office Conversion)
cases.applicant: Property ownership represented by Trevor Tunnel; tenant Juan de Saguar (Boses computer repair)

timeline.summary: The applicant sought to increase an existing 12-space parking variance to 21 spaces (9 additional) to convert 1,698 sq ft of warehouse space to office use for a computer-repair tenant with five employees, citing an overall building-wide parking shortfall (87 required vs. 66 existing) driven by code changes to parking ratios over time for other, previously-grandfathered tenants. Ed Lashins calculated that the specific use change at issue only required about 5 additional spaces (not 9) once the space's prior warehouse-parking credit was subtracted, arguing the applicant was using the opportunity to correct unrelated legacy shortfalls; the applicant's representative maintained that any new application triggers full code compliance for the whole site. The board ultimately voted to approve the full 21-space variance as requested.

cases.name: 12 Seymour Place — Land Coverage & FAR Variance (Accessory Garage/Barn)
cases.applicant: Represented by Paul Fusco (Lewis Fusco landscape architects)

timeline.summary: Applicants sought a 988-sq-ft land coverage variance and an 876-sq-ft accessory-structure FAR variance (36% over the 25%-of-main-house limit) to build a detached garage/barn, pool, and pavilion on an irregularly-shaped, narrow-entry lot, having considered and rejected an attached-garage alternative as creating access and massing problems. Neighbors raised drainage concerns via a submitted video and letters; the applicant's engineer described an expanded stormwater (cul-tech) system still being finalized with the town's engineering consultant but had not shared the specific plan with objecting neighbors. The board approved on the condition that the variance is contingent on the planning board/town engineer approving a satisfactory drainage plan protecting neighboring properties, and encouraged the applicant to share plans directly with concerned neighbors.

cases.name: 146/150/154 Lafayette Avenue — Parking Backing-Out Variance
cases.applicant: Manny Janas, represented by Douglas Cooper

timeline.summary: A repeat of a variance type the board had granted at 111 Lafayette Avenue two months earlier, allowing vehicles to back onto the street from perpendicular parking. No changes to the building were proposed; board members noted the recurring nature of this issue along the Lafayette Avenue industrial corridor. Approved unanimously with no objections (the only "neighbors" present were fellow applicants from a related property).

cases.name: 126 Lafayette Avenue — Front Yard Setback Variance (Auto Repair Shop / Solar Installation)
cases.applicant: Julio Rizzo (D&V Auto Repair), represented by James Glover (Green Hybrid Energy Solutions)

timeline.summary: The applicant needed a variance to legalize an existing, decades-old garage wall encroaching on the 25-foot front setback (identified only when applying to install rooftop solar panels), as a prerequisite to enclosing an exterior repair bay and adding two more bays flush with the building for the solar array. The wall's position long predated the current owner's 2000 purchase and no exterior alterations were proposed to the noncompliant wall itself; the board found the variance non-substantial given it merely legalized a pre-existing condition, and approved unanimously.

cases.name: 4 Nichols Road — Front Yard Setback Variance (Porch Addition)
cases.applicant: Homeowner ("Nick"), represented by architect Christian Aspenol (Steven Seek Architect)

timeline.summary: A small (2.89-foot) front-yard variance for a 391-sq-ft porch addition on a dead-end street, sized deliberately to be the minimum practical footprint. No neighbor objections were raised; the board found the ask minimal relative to the 50-foot code requirement and approved unanimously.

cases.name: 84 Business Park Drive — Parking Variance (Medical Office Conversion)
cases.applicant: Building ownership (presented by Ed Lashins' son)

timeline.summary: A 60,000-sq-ft office building sought a 4-space parking variance (242 existing vs. 246 required under the town's medical-use formula) to lease 3,700 sq ft to a White Plains Hospital-affiliated concierge medical practice with three practitioners and roughly seven staff. Board members found the shortfall non-substantial given ample existing surplus parking and a 40-plus-year history without parking shortages at the building, and approved unanimously; Ed Lashins recused himself throughout given a financial interest in the applicant and that the presenter was his son.

cases.name: 7 Palmer Place — Rear Yard Setback & Land Coverage Variance (Pool Patio)
cases.applicant: Anthony and Deanna [surname not clearly captured], represented by architect Stephen Holmes

timeline.summary: A code-compliant pool had an attached patio expanded during construction that encroached to within 30 feet of the 40-foot rear setback and pushed land coverage about 4% over the limit; the applicant said the overage stemmed from a misunderstanding that patio area attached to a pool counted toward the setback the same as a structure. Extensive replanting/screening (green giants, boxwoods) and a supportive adjacent neighbor were cited; the board found both variances non-substantial and approved unanimously.

cases.name: 258 East Middle Patent Road — Barn Replacement Variances (Accessible ADU)

timeline.summary: Applicants sought four variances (side-yard setback of 13.7 feet, an accessory-structure size roughly 70% of the principal dwelling versus a 25% limit, plus land coverage and height) to replace a structurally-unsalvageable 100-plus-year-old barn in essentially the same footprint, adding an ADA-accessible ground floor and bathroom so their adult son Tucker, who uses a power wheelchair and requires round-the-clock aide assistance, can visit and stay with dedicated space, plus a loft bedroom for his aide. All neighbors who share the driveway or are otherwise affected submitted letters of support, and the board found the size overage justified by the specific accessibility need (explicitly distinguishing it from a typical rental-unit ADU concern) and the site's physical constraints (bedrock, a tree the family wanted to preserve). The board approved all four variances.

cases.name: 8 East Lane — Side Yard Setback Variance (New Construction)

timeline.summary: A 2-foot side-yard variance (23 feet vs. 25-foot requirement) was needed after a final survey revealed a discrepancy from the original engineer's survey on a newly-constructed home, one of four lots in a recent subdivision. There was some board confusion locating the property and the ZBA notice sign relative to the cul-de-sac lots, but no neighbors objected (the affected side has no adjacent house yet); the board found the variance non-substantial, self-created, and with no environmental or character impact, and approved unanimously.

cases.name: 34 Kisco Avenue — Off-Street Parking Variance (Two-Family Home)

timeline.summary: Applicant sought to legalize the long-standing two-family use of a home in the "Peaceful Kingdom" area of Kisco Avenue by formalizing tandem/informal parking arrangements (5 spaces serving 2 units, some behind others) that a prior planning review had flagged as "blocked" access. The family has owned the two-family home since 1964 with no history of parking problems or street parking; the board found the variance non-substantial and approved unanimously.

cases.name: 19 Maryland Avenue — Front Yard Setback Variance (Survey Correction)

timeline.summary: A follow-up to a prior year's variance (previously approved at 12.75 feet) after an updated survey identified an existing enclosed porch's actual encroachment as 11.4 feet; no physical changes had been made to the structure since a decades-old (circa 1953) survey error was corrected. The board, having already made its five-factor findings on the underlying porch enclosure previously, treated this as a technical correction and approved unanimously.

cases.name: Pool & Patio Rear Yard Setback Variance (Santa Becky Residence)

timeline.summary: A continued hearing (revised from a prior meeting) for a rear-yard setback variance (34 feet into a 40-foot setback) for an in-ground pool, patio, and pool equipment on a sloped, wooded lot near North Lake Drive and Evergreen Row. The applicant relocated and enclosed the pool equipment against the pool shed with fencing to address neighbor noise concerns raised previously, and presented decibel estimates showing the equipment would be inaudible at the distances involved. A neighbor at 20 Evergreen Row did not oppose the pool itself but raised concerns about setting a precedent for future variance requests in the surrounded neighborhood and about future "people noise" (as opposed to equipment noise) from pool use; she asked for more specificity on vegetation buffering and fencing. The board found all five variance criteria satisfied (self-created, not substantial relative to unique topography/rock constraints, no environmental or neighborhood-character impact, no feasible alternative given prior design iterations) and approved unanimously, with an informal request that the applicant and neighbor work out any future noise issues directly.

cases.name: 125 Business Park Drive — Renewal of Prior Variances
cases.applicant: Nicole Ferrari (on behalf of Mike Ferrari, current property owner)

timeline.summary: A straightforward renewal of three variances originally granted in 2004 that had lapsed after not being renewed through several changes of ownership; the applicant sought renewal with no physical changes to what was previously approved. The board agreed to renew but dropped two of the original conditions that were no longer applicable or verifiable — a reference to an undated/unlocated 2003 conceptual planting plan, and a DEC wetlands-permit condition that will need to be independently re-obtained from DEC — deferring screening/landscaping conditions to the Planning Board's concurrent review instead. Ed Lashins recused himself (he owns nearby buildings on Business Park Drive, is a former owner of the subject property, and was involved in the original approval).

cases.name: 113 King Street — Toll Brothers Entrance Signage Variances
cases.applicant: Toll Brothers (represented by attorney Kevney Moses)

timeline.summary: Toll Brothers sought three signage variances for the entrance to its approved 125-townhome / mixed residential redevelopment (10% affordable) on a site rezoned from DOB to RMFA: two signs where one is allowed and a 4.5-foot setback where five is required (both attorney-argued as pre-existing legally-grandfathered nonconformities under the town code's grandfathering provision), plus a substantive request to increase existing sign height by 1'10". Rather than have the board interpret the grandfathering question, the applicant elected to simply request variance approval on all three items for simplicity, which the board granted after confirming the signage was tastefully scaled, matched surrounding-property signage sizes, and served wayfinding needs for a 55-mph roadway; the ARB had already approved the sign design in December 2025 contingent on variance approval.

cases.name: 45 Rolling Cam(p) Drive — Gross Land Coverage Variance (Hard-Surface Tennis Court)
cases.applicant: 45 Rolling Cam LLC (represented by attorney Jerry Tortarella of Hockerman, Tortarella & Wekstein)

timeline.summary: Applicant sought a 7,622-square-foot gross land coverage variance to complete a sunken, walled hard-surface tennis court on an over-10-acre Conyers Farm estate lot, previously approved by the Planning Board as part of a larger build-out but pushed over the coverage limit once field changes (widened/straightened driveways, additional parking-court area, stone walls/walkways not originally counted) were factored in. Counsel argued the tennis court is not visible off-site (sunk 8-10 feet below grade, screened by mature evergreen buffer planted early in construction), has no stormwater or environmental impact (drainage already engineered to existing devices), and that a grass-court alternative would not meet the owner's stated need for a surface usable across ages/skill levels. The Planning Board had already approved the underlying field changes in January 2026. The board found no adverse impact to the neighborhood or environment and approved unanimously with no public opposition.

cases.name: 9 [ASR: "Milton"] Avenue — Two-Family Conversion: Floor Area & Parking Variances
cases.address: 9 [Milton] Avenue (ASR-uncertain street name; heard as "nine of them on Avenue")
cases.lastStatus: partially granted (floor area variance approved; parking variance tabled)

trajectory.status: partially granted (floor area variance approved; parking variance tabled)

timeline.status: partially granted (floor area variance approved; parking variance tabled)
timeline.summary: The Fredericks sought two variances to formalize a long-standing (since 2017 purchase, believed two-family since acquisition) two-family use after a building-inspector review found no certificate of occupancy for two families: a floor-area variance for a ~400-square-foot roofline raise (removing dormers to make second-floor space usable), and a parking variance to permit four required spaces where the existing driveway realistically fits about three cars without stacking into the street. Neighbors submitted letters raising a real, board-acknowledged on-street parking problem (no legal street parking near a fire hydrant, tight lots, houses close together). The board closed the floor-area portion and approved it unanimously, but kept the parking-variance public hearing open and declined to rule on it, telling the applicant it could not approve the parking variance as presented and inviting them to return with engineer/architect-documented parking alternatives (e.g., squeezing a legal third or fourth space) before a future session.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge Townhouses — Clubhouse Parking Variance
cases.applicant: Eagle Ridge developer/ownership entity (represented by land use counsel, on behalf of an 88-unit townhouse project)

timeline.summary: As a condition of its 2023 master site-plan approval, the 88-unit Eagle Ridge townhouse project (80 market-rate, 8 affordable, plus rental/condo units) had to return to the ZBA for its clubhouse design. An enlarged clubhouse (expanded from ~2,100 sq ft with just a pool to include pickleball/bocce courts and a second story) increased the required parking from an originally-anticipated 26 spaces to 51, and the Planning Board barred use of on-street visitor spaces once the clubhouse grew — producing a 25-space (49%) parking variance request. Counsel argued the project's overall parking supply is ample in totality (352 resident spaces plus 30 visitor spaces plus the 26 clubhouse spaces) and that adding clubhouse parking would require sacrificing required open space on a steep slope adjacent to a community park, increasing impervious surface and runoff. The board agreed the deficiency was offset by the project's overall parking surplus and self-contained, walkable layout, and approved unanimously.

cases.name: 435 Main Street — Bank Signage Replacement Variance
cases.applicant: Bank branch (represented by sign installer, Sign Star)

timeline.summary: A bank branch sought variances to replace existing, already-nonconforming signage in kind: three wall signs where two are allowed (existing legal nonconformity, unchanged in count), and three directional signs at roughly 6 square feet each where code allows 1 square foot (also an existing nonconformity). The replacements are essentially a cosmetic refresh — same illumination (existing goose-neck lighting reused, non-illuminated directionals), slightly larger dimensions on the two side wall signs (about one foot longer) and a smaller front wall sign, plus a decorative skirt added around the directional sign posts. No new signs were being added. After confirming no signage count or illumination changes were involved, the board approved unanimously.

cases.name: 8 Hollow Ridge Road — Patio/Outdoor Kitchen Gross Land Coverage & Drainage Variance
cases.applicant: Jennifer Drucker (represented by attorney Katie Wendell and designer Nick [Glengate Company])

timeline.summary: Applicant sought to replace a deteriorating patio with new patio space, add a fireplace, and enlarge an outdoor kitchen in the same footprint, netting only a 63-square-foot increase in impervious surface — but the underlying lot was already substantially over its gross land coverage allowance (roughly 21,315 of 14,551 permitted square feet, a variance of about 6,826.8 sq ft) due to pre-existing hardscape installed by a prior owner before the current owner's purchase 1.5 years ago. One board member pushed back hard on characterizing the addition as merely "63 square feet," repeatedly pressing on the legality of the pre-existing coverage, unresolved town-engineer (KSCJ/Adam Kaufman) drainage comments about tying into a nonexistent mitigation system, and initially refused to vote to approve without a direct letter from the town engineer, pushing to table the matter. The impasse was resolved when the Building Inspector (Rob) was reached by phone and confirmed on the record that any board-imposed drainage-mitigation conditions would be enforced through the building-permit/RPRC review process regardless of ZBA sign-off. The board then approved the variance conditioned on the applicant satisfying the town engineer's and building inspector's drainage-mitigation requirements before a building permit issues.

cases.name: 69 James Street — Modification of Previously-Approved Addition (Bedroom Extension in Lieu of Basement)

timeline.summary: The applicants previously received variance and building-permit approval for a home addition, but found excavating a basement infeasible and costly due to bedrock on the site. In lieu of the basement, they proposed extending a bedroom approximately 2.5 feet further toward the street (not toward any neighbor or sight line), for additional storage/living space for their teenage son, without altering any of the previously-approved variance dimensions. A neighbor across the street (Joelle) submitted an updated letter reiterating support, consistent with a letter she wrote for the original approval. The board found the change self-created but non-substantial, with no environmental or neighborhood-character impact and no feasible alternative other than building upward (which the applicants noted would raise other height/setback issues on their corner, 1929-era lot), and approved unanimously.
